## What

Wiring `@papercusp/failure-detector` (φ-accrual + SWIM `indirectProbe` +
`decideEviction`) into the lock authority so a crashed authority is evicted before
the 90s staleness window (`shared-pot-hardening-2026-06-13` P-016,
`packages/operator-core/lib/authority/peer-eviction.ts`). Two non-obvious traps,
each of which would silently break correctness if wired the naive way.

## Trap 1 — `decideEviction` reads "all relays unreachable" as "confirmed dead"

The README snippet is `decideEviction(detector.phi(now), await indirectProbe(...))`.
But `decideEviction`'s contract is: `phi < threshold` → keep; `indirect == null` →
evict (`no-relays-high-phi`); `indirect.alive` → keep; **else → evict
(`confirmed-dead`)**. That final `else` fires whenever the probe result is "not
alive" — and an `IndirectProbeResult` where every relay landed in the
`unreachable` bucket (no `confirmedBy`, no `deadBy`) is "not alive". So a naive
wiring **evicts a live authority whenever YOUR transport is down / addressing
isn't wired / there are no reachable relays** — i.e. exactly the pre-addressing
state, the common one. That's a false-positive eviction caused by our OWN
blindness, not the target being dead.

**Fix:** gate on a real signal before trusting `confirmed-dead`. Only evict early
when at least one REACHABLE relay failed to vouch:

```ts
const result = await indirectProbe(target, relays, probe, { k: 3, label: peerLabel });
if (result.confirmedBy.length === 0 && result.deadBy.length === 0) {
  return { evict: false, reason: 'alive-direct' }; // all relays unreachable → inconclusive, KEEP
}
return decideEviction(phi, result, threshold); // alive-indirect (keep) | confirmed-dead (evict)
```

This is deliberately STRICTER than the lib's bare-φ `no-relays-high-phi`/`confirmed-dead`
options: with no witness we keep the peer and let the 90s staleness floor handle it
(fail-open, D-004, unchanged). A witness must agree before we evict early.

## Trap 2 — a relay-side authority op must be authority-EXEMPT

The SWIM relay probe is a `peer.probe` RPC asking *another* peer "is X alive from
your view?". It rides the same `PeerRpcTransport` + `handleAuthorityRpc` dispatch
as the file-lock ops — but `handleAuthorityRpc` runs `verifyIsAuthority` for every
kind, and a RELAY is not (necessarily) the elected authority. So a naive
registration makes every relay reply `not_authority`, which the prober's transport
maps to `PeerUnreachableError` → the relay lands in the `unreachable` bucket → no
signal ever → eviction never works.

**Fix:** mark the op authority-exempt so the dispatch skips `verifyIsAuthority` for
it (the caller-signature/EI-322 gate still applies):

```ts
registerAuthorityOp(PEER_PROBE_OP_KIND, handler, { authorityExempt: true });
```

`handleAuthorityRpc` consults the global exempt set (`getAuthorityExemptKinds()`),
so this works over BOTH the HTTP route and the Hyperswarm-mux transport
(`authority-rpc-swarm-wiring.ts` dispatches through the same `handleAuthorityRpc`,
no per-rig `authorityExemptKinds` needed). A multi-instance rig that passes its own
`handlers` map must pass `authorityExemptKinds` explicitly (it bypasses the global
registry).

## Why it matters

Both traps fail SILENTLY — no error, just "eviction never fires" (trap 2) or
"eviction fires constantly when we're blind" (trap 1). The keep-by-default safety
policy (trap 1) is also what keeps the feature non-regressing: single box / no
transport → no eviction → byte-identical to staleness-only selection. The LIVE
cross-machine proof is real-hardware-gated (D-003); the deterministic path is
proven in `authority/__tests__/peer-eviction.test.ts` + `peer-probe-op.test.ts`.
